title: 1976: The Soweto Uprising
summary: Bantu Education and the Afrikaans Medium Decree, Black Consciousness and Steve Biko, the events of 16 June 1976, and the effects of the uprising.

notes.text: Under the **Bantu Education Act (1953)**, schools for black learners were badly funded. In 1975 the government spent about R644 a year on each white learner but only about R42 on each black learner. Classes were overcrowded, many teachers were under-qualified, and there were few textbooks.

In the late 1960s **Steve Biko** and others founded the **South African Students' Organisation (SASO)** and the **Black Consciousness Movement (BCM)**. Black Consciousness taught that black people must free themselves from feelings of inferiority, take pride in their identity and history, and lead their own struggle. These ideas inspired many high-school learners in the 1970s.

notes.label: Quote
notes.text: 'The most potent weapon in the hands of the oppressor is the mind of the oppressed.' (Steve Biko)

In **1974** the government ordered that from Standard 5 (Grade 7) onwards, half of all subjects in black schools, including mathematics and social studies, had to be taught in **Afrikaans**. Learners and many teachers did not speak Afrikaans well, and many saw it as the 'language of the oppressor'.

notes.title: Why this rule caused such anger
notes.problem: Why did the Afrikaans Medium Decree of 1974 lead to protest?
steps: It forced certain subjects to be taught in Afrikaans.
Many pupils and teachers did not speak it well, so learning suffered.
Afrikaans was seen as the language of the oppressor.
notes.answer: It harmed learning and was linked to apartheid.

items: Learners formed the **Soweto Students' Representative Council**, led by **Tsietsi Mashinini**, and planned a peaceful protest march.
On the morning of **16 June 1976**, between 10 000 and 20 000 learners marched towards **Orlando Stadium**, carrying placards such as 'Down with Afrikaans'.
Police blocked the march near Orlando West High School. They fired tear gas and then live bullets into the crowd.

**Hector Pieterson**, aged 12 or 13, was one of the first to be killed. A photograph by **Sam Nzima** showed him being carried by Mbuyisa Makhubo, with his sister **Antoinette Sithole** running beside them.
Learners responded by burning government buildings and beer halls. The unrest spread to other parts of the country.

notes.text: By the end of 1977, more than **500 people** (some estimates are much higher) had been killed, many of them children, and thousands were injured or detained.

items: The Afrikaans Medium Decree was withdrawn.
Thousands of young people left the country to join the ANC and PAC in exile and train as MK soldiers.
The photograph of Hector Pieterson shocked the world and increased international pressure on apartheid.
In 1977 the government banned Black Consciousness organisations. Steve Biko died in police custody in **September 1977** after being brutally assaulted; the UN imposed a mandatory **arms embargo**.
The uprising showed the power of young people in the struggle. **16 June** is now **Youth Day**.

notes.title: Source L: A placard carried on 16 June 1976 (as recorded in photographs)
notes.text: IF WE MUST DO AFRIKAANS, VORSTER MUST DO ZULU

notes.title: Short-term and long-term effects
notes.problem: Give one short-term and one long-term effect of 16 June 1976.
steps: Short-term: unrest spread across the country and hundreds were killed.
Long-term: many young people left to join the ANC and PAC abroad, and the world increased its pressure on South Africa.
notes.answer: Nationwide protest, and a stronger liberation movement.
